Tragedy on the Nepal-Tibet border. Plus: How Mark Carney stood up to Trump

Get the Guardian Weekly delivered to your home address

Over the last week, the world has watched with horror the scenes from the Tibet-Nepal border where a devastating torrent of mud, water and ice tore along the Bhotekoshi River, destroying entire communities and leaving more than 1,000 people dead and several thousand more missing.

From the Nepali town of Devighat, our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen describes a nightmarish scene of overflowing mortuaries and unidentifiable bodies, as shellshocked survivors of the flood slowly return to the ruins of their homes.

The disaster happened after the collapse of a glacier – and while global heating has not been definitively attributed as the cause, it is undeniable that steep mountain slopes and valleys are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, while extreme weather events such as monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate breakdown, as our global environment writer Jonathan Watts explains.

Then columnist Nesrine Malik paints a wider picture and argues that while for many people these floods may feel as though they have happened a world away, the climate crisis is coming for us all, one way or another.

stories.title: Spending deal comes with a bonus: Blocking political control of grants
stories.summary: Congress pauses the OMB's attempt to rewrite how research is funded.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Congress pauses the OMB’s attempt to rewrite how research is funded.

On Tuesday, the House of Representatives passed a stopgap measure that would continue funding the US government through early December. While the measure still requires the signature of President Trump, it’s widely expected that he will act to avoid a government shutdown immediately before the midterm elections.

This is a normal part of how the US government has operated in recent years, as it’s often difficult to build the political support needed to pass a full year’s budget in advance. In fact, dissent within the House’s Republican caucus prevented them from agreeing on their own measure to keep the government open; instead, the House simply adopted a version of the spending bill that had previously passed the Senate.

From the perspective of scientists and their supporters, that adoption turned out to be a very good thing. Because the Senate’s budget bill, passed in early August , contains a provision that blocks the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) from implementing new rules that would give political appointees full control over what science is funded and allow them to cancel any grant at any time. The proposed rule has been widely decried as catastrophic for science, and it faced widespread opposition from scientific and health-focused organizations.

That opposition likely contributed to two senators, Patty Murray (D-Wash.) and Susan Collins (R-Maine), inserting language into the budget deal that prevents the OMB from implementing it prior to the expiration of the stopgap measure on December 11.

While this is not a permanent reprieve, it does signal that the legislature is not interested in handing OMB and other administration officials that much control over federal spending—the bill passed the Senate by a 90-6 margin, and by 370-48 in the House, where opposition largely focused on other aspects of the measure. Those margins raise the prospect that similar language could be inserted into any further budget deals without triggering opposition.

stories.title: Netherlands moves billions in gold to London in 'crisis preparedness' move
stories.summary: The Dutch central bank removes some of its gold reserves from the US and Canada, saying it is because of "increasing geopolitical unrest".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
While much of the gold was sold in New York and then repurchased in London, more than 27 tonnes was physically moved to the UK

Published 5 hours ago

The Dutch central bank (DNB) has confirmed that billions of dollars in gold has been taken out of north America and relocated to London, citing "increasing geopolitical unrest".

DNB said on Wednesday that 86 tonnes of gold had been removed from the US and Canada in a complex operation that took several months. It is now being held by the Bank of England, where the precious metal can be traded more easily "in a crisis situation".

Bank president Olaf Sleijpen said the move was "necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness".

The decision comes amid an ongoing trade dispute between the US and Canada, with both countries announcing fresh tariffs on each other after failed trade talks.

DNB said the transfer, which took place between March and August, saw 27 tonnes of gold bars moved from New York and Ottawa to Zeist in the Netherlands.

A similar quantity and quality was then moved to London, with no need to melt the bars down.

Exactly how so much gold was transported across the Atlantic Ocean has not been revealed.

The rest of the transfer was carried out by selling the gold in New York, and repurchasing it in London, the bank said , external .

"Combining the processes of buying and selling and physical transport has allowed DNB to spread the risks associated with such a complex physical gold relocation," the statement said.

DNB did not confirm what it was referring to with its mention of "geopolitical unrest" but the US economy remains in an uncertain position due to the country's ongoing war with Iran, which has impacted global trade.

Canada, meanwhile, has been hit hard by US tariffs on its key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles as well as an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods announced in August.

DNB said that gold that is held with the Bank of England "is regarded as the world's most easily tradable gold," and therefore more readily available in a crisis than if it was still in the US or Canada.

Prior to Wednesday's announcement, the DNB held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa. This has now fallen to 18.5% in both countries.

The total Dutch gold stock was 612.4 tonnes at the end of 2025 and has been valued at €72.2 billion, DNB said.

The bank's share of gold in London has increased from 18.1% to 32.1% after the move, while it still holds 30.8% of its reserves in the Netherlands.

stories.body:
The Conservative leader’s choice of a new shadow chancellor shows a lack of insight into the reasons why the party was defeated at the last election

T o outlast a prime minister always counts as some kind of achievement for an opposition leader, although Kemi Badenoch cannot claim credit for Sir Keir Starmer’s downfall . Sir Keir’s wounds were mostly self-inflicted. To the extent that opposition pressure was involved, it was electoral threats from Reform UK and the Green party that stoked Labour party frustration to a regicidal pitch. The Tory leader’s role was largely as a spectator.

Mrs Badenoch still hopes to use regime change to her advantage. She thinks the economy, and fiscal discipline in particular, will be her most fruitful line of attack. In their first confrontation at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the Conservative leader called Mr Burnham a “spendthrift” and “people pleaser” who will dodge the tough decisions required to prove Britain’s creditworthiness on international markets. She expects him to yield to Labour MPs’ demands for budget increases, which will then have to be financed with tax rises.

In that scenario, Mrs Badenoch imagines a vacancy for a rehabilitated small-state Conservative party offering hard-headed budget management, less profligate than Labour; more sober and respectable than Reform UK. That message would unite what remains of her depleted party. She can’t compete with Nigel Farage on the terrain of anti-immigrant rhetoric (although that doesn’t stop her aping his stances ). She shows no interest in finding political accommodation for socially liberal, pro-European one-nation Tories who now have more in common with the Liberal Democrats than the modern Conservative party.

This leaves the Tories with a narrow focus on tax cuts, reining in welfare spending and deregulation as a spur to enterprise. Mr Farage supports those things too, but Mrs Badenoch believes that Reform UK’s maverick style and the whiff of impropriety around its financial dealings make it an unreliable vehicle for a classically Thatcherite agenda that belongs, by rights, to Lady Thatcher’s own party.

The claim to be the true keeper of the Thatcherite flame has become a ritual for Tory leaders. The mantle has passed through so many hands, it is threadbare as a political definition in 2026. It was worn most preposterously by Liz Truss, who posted photos of herself on social media recreating iconic images of the Iron Lady in her pomp. She then detonated her government with a “ mini-budget ” that was a crass pastiche of the economic ideas she claimed to venerate – a wild foray into fiscal irresponsibility masquerading as free-market radicalism.

One of the Treasury ministers who enthusiastically endorsed Ms Truss’s plan, Andrew Griffith, was this week appointed Mrs Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor. He replaces Mel Stride, a lower-octane performer who was deemed not to have made sufficient impact in the role. It is a revealing choice that undermines the Tory leader’s plan to make economic competence the centrepiece of her pitch to lead the nation. When considering a potential chancellor, she clearly values the ability to grab attention over economic judgment.

This is consistent with a pattern of failure to engage with the full spectrum of failures over many years that accounts for the scale of Tory defeat at the last election. What Mrs Badenoch imagines to be a political strategy looks more like retreat to an ideological comfort zone in the hope that a second prime minister will self-destruct while she watches from the sidelines.

stories.title: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge
stories.summary: The PM said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as he faced Kemi Badenoch at Prime Minister's Questions for the first time.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 September 2026, 14:15 BST

Andy Burnham said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as his first Prime Minister's Questions took place against a backdrop of rising UK borrowing costs.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to say where spending would be cut and how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high on Wednesday.

He blamed the previous Tory government, saying the "turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they left behind".

Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July before Parliament's summer recess, meaning Wednesday was the first time he had faced Badenoch at PMQs.

Burnham sought to stress his administration's fiscal responsibility and said ministers were taking steps to reduce debt.

He told MPs: "This will be a government grounded in fiscal responsibility. It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost-of-living pressure on our constituents, and that's the approach that we will take."

Interest rates on government bonds have been going up, with the yield on a 10-year bond at its highest level since 2008, while the yield on a 30-year bond is at its highest since 1998.

This means it costs the government more to borrow over the long term and could constrain its spending choices as the 28 October Budget approaches.

Burnham's PMQs debut came after he used the summer recess to tour the UK, announcing a series of eye-catching policies mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.

On Wednesday, Badenoch said the prime minister had set out plenty of spending plans but no detail of how he would be paying the bill.

"The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from," she said.

"He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice - higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts.

"Yesterday he said change begins with honesty, so will he be honest and tell us: is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?"

Burnham had earlier said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and a cut in business rates for hospitality.

"I've already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I'm not going to do what any prime minister has done and write the budget here," he said, adding he and Chancellor John Healey had agreed on an earlier date for the Budget to reduce speculation.

In the Commons, Badenoch also raised comments from economist and cross-bench peer Lord Jim O'Neill, who had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser, but who ruled out joining Burnham's government .

Speaking to the BBC, Lord O'Neill had praised the PM for "a great first five weeks" which he said had helped lift consumer and business confidence; adding the current spike in market interest rates for government debt would force Labour to start "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Badenoch pointed to a warning from Lord O'Neill that the prime minister's tone during his Tuesday Commons debut would have unsettled investors, although the peer had also said that spike was mostly mirroring US market upheaval concerning the Iran conflict.

Kemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons at PMQs

"Lord O'Neill, a close friend of the prime minister, said yesterday's statement in the Commons was the last thing investors wanted to hear," Badenoch said.

"Lord O'Neill is a serious economist. He knows what he's talking about and, sure enough, yesterday the cost of government borrowing rose to its highest in 18 years.

"How does he plan to tackle the government's rising debt costs?"

Burnham replied that he and Lord O'Neill did "not always agree", before attacking Badenoch's shadow cabinet reshuffle for bringing MPs who were in the leadership team of former Conservative prime minister Liz Truss back to her front benches.

To shouts of "point-scoring!" from the Conservative side, he said: "Can I also say to her and the whole of her new shadow cabinet, the majority of whom were part of a government that lasted for 49 days, a short-lived government that crashed confidence in the economy and hammered people's mortgages.

"She took a decision at the weekend, she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini budget was a mistake, and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped to write the Truss mini budget."

In the Tory reshuffle , Andrew Griffith replaced Sir Mel Stride as shadow chancellor.

Badenoch said Burnham had not ruled out tax rises, claiming: "The reason why that budget failed was because spending was announced before the money to pay for it, which is exactly what he is doing right now."

The opposition leader went on to raise the alleged Russian attack on Leipzig airport in Germany , urging the prime minister to commit to 3% spending.

So far the new government has only committed to meeting the 3.5% spending target for defence by 2035, pushing back the interim 3% spending commitment to spring next year.

The new chancellor quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, which proved to be the final nail in the coffin for Sir Keir's premiership.

Burnham told MPs: "The very reason I appointed this Chancellor to his position is because of his strong commitment to the defence of our country and to defence spending.

"We will fully fund the defence investment plan and at the spending review we will set out a plan to meet the Nato commitments by 2035, there is no problem with our commitment to defence."

stories.title: Trump may be forced to reveal secret rules feds use for AI safety testing
stories.summary: Trump’s secret reviews of frontier AI models may hide corruption, lawsuit says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump’s secret reviews of frontier AI models may hide corruption, lawsuit says.

Four federal agencies have been sued amid calls to release information about the secret framework that the Trump administration uses to conduct safety reviews of frontier AI models prior to release.

In a Wednesday press release announcing the lawsuit, a nonpartisan nonprofit called Protect Democracy alleged that “almost no details” have been released to the public or Congress. To everyone except a few vague “trusted partners,” it remains unclear what the government’s review process looks like, which companies are involved in constructing the framework, or what legal authority Trump officials have to conduct the reviews.

“Neither the identities of those entities nor the criteria by which they were selected have been made public,” Protect Democracy said.

That’s a problem, Protect Democracy alleged in a statement to Ars, since decisions about “which AI models are approved and released may be the most important policy question of this White House.” And it appears that at least one AI firm, OpenAI, has “negotiated a private agreement with the Federal Government to limit distribution of its cutting-edge AI models to government-vetted partners.”

The group’s lawsuit is seeking an order requiring officials to produce all information sought by September 30. That includes “unclassified procedural and contractual architecture: the framework’s text, the terms of participation, the identity of participants, and the process and criteria by which access to frontier models is granted or withheld,” the complaint said. They also want an injunction restraining officials from improperly withholding records that aren’t classified.

“The executive branch is now choosing which companies can release their products and which customers get access to a technology that could shape the future of not only American industry and national security, but economies and governments abroad as well,” Protect Democracy’s release said. “All with no oversight from Congress, the public, or tech experts outside of the executive branch.”

Secret rules allegedly hide corruption

According to Protect Democracy, the framework could potentially be “corrupt,” with officials from the Office of the National Cyber Director, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the Treasury Department, and the Commerce Department potentially favoring rapid deployments for AI firms that Trump likes. And on the flip side, the public has already seen Trump retaliate against an AI firm for being too woke, Protect Democracy noted, pointing to a judge’s recent ruling that it was illegal for Trump to blacklist Anthropic .

As AI technology advances and cybersecurity risks escalate— OpenAI’s model hacking Hugging Face is the most obvious recent example—the public can’t afford to blindly trust Trump to act in good faith when choosing which frontier models should be rigorously tested, Protect Democracy said. And perhaps even worse, the public cannot know if new vulnerabilities discovered in the real world are due to agencies failing to complete a proper review, running outdated or ineffective tests, missing important checks, or missing steps that align with the latest mitigation strategies advanced by leading AI safety experts.

“We deserve to know what’s in the framework,” the group said, joining other calls for the agencies to be more transparent about AI model deployments.

In a post on X last month, US Representative Greg Casar (D-Tx.) accused Trump of “completely failing to keep us safe from the dangers of AI” while taking “millions from AI billionaires.”

“Now, in the wake of extremely dangerous AI cybersecurity problems, he says he’s set up ‘voluntary’ review that no one has seen,” Casar said. “Asleep at the wheel. Too busy cashing in to protect our jobs or national security.”

More recently, another Democrat, California state Senator Josh Becker, urged the court to grant Protect Democracy’s request. In a declaration supporting their complaint, Becker noted that California is mulling a bill, SB 813 , that would establish a process where independent organizations would set baselines for AI safety standards. If passed—unlike Trump’s approach—California’s plan would make the latest benchmarks, standards, and methodologies used to evaluate risks posed by AI systems transparent to the public, Becker said. Already, public input has shaped the bill, he noted, with one provision withdrawn following public backlash.

“In contrast to the Administration’s approach, every step of SB 813’s development has been public,” Becker wrote, emphasizing that “we are accountable for the framework we have set.”

No one knows Trump’s “trusted partners”

The Trump administration has been rushing to set up the voluntary safety review process ever since the government flagged Anthropic’s Mythos 5 model as too dangerous to release earlier this summer. The plan was to rapidly expand industry collaborations so that government teams at the Center for AI Standards and Innovation could review prerelease models with reduced or removed safeguards to “thoroughly evaluate national security-related capabilities and risks.” But that would be impossible, Trump realized, without industry experts being fully transparent and explaining what exactly new models could do.

In July, the White House launched a clearinghouse, GOLD EAGLE , that relies on industry partners to help agencies flag cybersecurity vulnerabilities across many sectors and industries. Again, Protect Democracy noted that the “White House did not identify any company participating in GOLD EAGLE, the terms on which they are participating, or any legal authority for the program.”

Then, on August 3, the White House announced that it had completed the voluntary framework for reviewing AI models before their public release. Both the framework and GOLD EAGLE are actively being used to review frontier models as the technology advances, the White House has confirmed.

Some parts of the government’s review process are classified. The executive order explained that Trump planned to develop “a classified benchmarking process” that would assess advanced capabilities of AI models and determine when models should be designated as frontier AI.

However, Protect Democracy’s complaint said the framework itself is notably not designated as classified. Despite that, the White House has refused to share details with the public. Instead, a spokesperson told reporters that “just because things are unclassified, that doesn’t mean we are going to broadcast them to everyone.”

Additionally concerning, the term “covered frontier model” is not defined, Protect Democracy said. If the definition is too narrow, some dangerous AI models could slip through the cracks, and if it’s too broad, agencies recently gutted by DOGE cuts may be spread too thin to assess too many models at once. Without more clarity, the public “can only hope this powerful technology is being governed safely and in the public interest,” Protect Democracy alleged.

So far, the framework has only been shared with “a select set of AI companies,” which excludes meaningful stakeholders, such as AI safety groups currently warning of emerging societal risks, as well as smaller or emerging AI firms whose input or model reviews may be just as critical.

Protect Democracy regularly relies on making FOIA requests in its mission to “prevent American democracy from declining into a more authoritarian form of government,” the complaint said. Fearing that Trump was seizing too much power over AI, the group sent identical FOIA requests to four US agencies, urgently seeking only non-classified information and requesting that their request be expedited. So far, no agency has produced any records, the complaint said. Only the National Cyber Director’s office responded, but it denied the group’s request to expedite the process, which Protect Democracy is now challenging as improper.

Congress is in the dark, too

On top of leaving the public in the dark—and independent researchers, advocacy groups, AI investors, and businesses in many industries with a stake in AI—lawmakers have been blocked from assessing the executive branch’s AI safety framework.

That matters, Protect Democracy alleged, because Trump’s AI safety operation may be destabilized if Congress is not on the same page. Right now, Congress is mulling whether to renew the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act (CISA) of 2015, which seemingly is the sole legal basis allowing AI firms to share information with the government through GOLD EAGLE, the complaint said.

Those protections are part of a CISA provision that lapsed once, and Congress must soon decide if the provision should be extended. There’s discord between the House of Representatives and the Senate on the deadline to vote on the extension, but the earliest that could happen is September 30 and the latest is December 11.

“In either event, Congress will soon need to decide whether to extend CISA’s liability protections that, by the administration’s own account, sustain the GOLD EAGLE program that the administration has announced but has yet to explain,” Protect Democracy’s complaint said. “Indeed, a senior administration official publicly acknowledged at GOLD EAGLE’s launch that, absent that reauthorization, ‘this effort is fundamentally challenged.’”

Deana El-Mallawany, director of Impact Programs & Counsel at Protect Democracy, told Ars that “neither Protect Democracy nor Congress has enough information about the GOLD EAGLE program to make a fully informed decision on extending CISA. Our concern is that the White House is putting Congress in the position of voting on a CISA extension without knowing how the GOLD EAGLE program is operating, who’s involved, or what statutory authority is being invoked. That’s why we’re seeking these records.”

Protect Democracy alleged that without these records, the Trump administration could escape accountability for AI safety review.

“Congress cannot meaningfully oversee programs whose terms and asserted authority it has not been shown” and “courts cannot review action they cannot identify,” the complaint said.

El-Mallawany told Ars that if Protect Democracy gets access to the framework, all documents will be posted publicly. Without more transparency, the list of concerns that Protect Democracy has about Trump’s potential ability to leverage the voluntary framework over the AI industry is long , El-Mallawany said, adding:

The risks are abundant, including the risk that the White House could use the secret process to coerce AI companies over decisions like whether to deploy AI for lethal autonomous weapons and mass surveillance (as we saw with the clash between the Pentagon and Anthropic), to extort certain investors and employees for political and financial support or punish others for perceived political opposition, or to force AI companies to incorporate politicized viewpoints into their models—not to mention the risk that the review framework is simply ineffective, creating a false sense of security.

stories.title: Taiwan’s six-year hunt for China’s undercover chip labs
stories.summary: Previously unpublished government data reveals the scale of Taiwan’s crackdown on Chinese companies accused of hiding their ties while recruiting chip talent and pursuing sensitive technology.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Features

Previously unpublished government data reveals the scale of Taiwan’s crackdown on Chinese companies accused of hiding their ties while recruiting chip talent and pursuing sensitive technology.

I n the spring of 2020, a Taiwanese engineer felt “extremely lucky” to be offered a job as a chip designer at Blue Ocean Smart System, an American company based in his hometown Hsinchu, the heart of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. He said the role gave him a chance to work on an ambitious AI-chip design project and a $120,000 salary, doubling the industry average, which would help pay off his two children’s private elementary education.

But several months into his new role, the engineer, who was 32 at the time, noticed something strange: He was never in touch with any American coworkers, and there was no information about the U.S. office. Instead, he told Rest of World , he spent most of his time working with team members based in Nanjing, China. That’s who he spoke with in weekly online meetings, and with whom he shared his engineering code and chip designs.

What followed confirmed the engineer’s suspicion: In August 2021, Taiwanese authorities raided Blue Ocean Smart System , alleging that the company illegally operated in Taiwan by disguising its Chinese ownership behind a locally registered company.

The Taiwan-registered company shared the exact same English name as Nanjing-based Blue Ocean Smart System, while its Chinese name differed by just one character. The Taiwan operation was later forced to shut down. Blue Ocean Smart System in Nanjing did not respond to Rest of World ’s requests for comment.

“I was explicitly told that the company was backed by American investment,” the engineer told Rest of World , recalling the inconsistencies he picked up during his time there. “But I kept going because I was happy at my job.”

Blue Ocean Smart System is one of the 166 cases investigated by Taiwanese authorities over the past six years for allegedly concealing ties to China, according to exclusive data provided to Rest of World by Taiwan’s Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau, or MJIB. Another 67 China-related trade-secret probes in the technology sector were completed in the same period, according to MJIB figures that have not previously been made public.

The crackdown remains active. As recently as August 5, the MJIB announced it had raided another 18 technology companies, following operations carried out just days earlier between July 13 and August 4.

Taiwan is a global powerhouse in chip manufacturing. Thanks to companies like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company — known as TSMC — Mediatek, and United Microelectronics Corporation, the island nation produces over 60% of the world’s semiconductors and 90% of the world’s most advanced chips. But the strength and vibrancy of the industry has also attracted unwanted interference, with Chinese competitors accused of illegal investments and talent poaching. Taiwan’s crackdown reflects a broader trend to limit China’s access to critical technology across the world, and in the U.S.

Almost everyone in the industry would know or have heard of people who were approached or worked for Chinese companies.” John Chen, a board director at Taiwan-listed chip design company MicroIP

In Taiwan, Chinese investments are scrutinized by a unique legal framework due to the political tensions between the two governments. Under the Cross-Strait Act and related investment regulations, Chinese companies — whether they’re a bubble tea shop or a tech company — are required to obtain government approval before operating on the self-ruled island.

Chinese companies have repeatedly skirted these regulations by operating outside official approval, setting up shell companies, or registering their operations under non-Chinese nationals.

Semicon Taiwan, Asia’s biggest semiconductor trade event, is held in Taiwan each September. Last year, over 100,000 industry professionals from 65 countries attended. Sam Yeh/AFP via Getty Images

Tai Yuen Hi-Tech Industrial Park in Hsinchu is home to approximately 300 companies. Lam Yik Fei for Rest of World

In 2020, Taiwan stepped up enforcement amid intensifying concerns over China’s tech industry from both Taiwanese and U.S. authorities. MJIB, the island’s equivalent of the FBI, kicked off a special operation involving all of its 2,000 investigators to look into Chinese-linked investments in its technology sector.

China has criticized these investigations as “political manipulation.” In 2022, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office spokesperson at the time, Ma Xiaoguang, accused Taiwan’s ruling party of “smearing and intimidating mainland enterprises in Taiwan” with raids that were “politically motivated attempts to obstruct” cooperation and would ultimately harm business interests.

Meanwhile, Taiwanese authorities say this Chinese business activity represents a risk to national security. This past April, Taiwan’s National Security Bureau published a report warning that China continues to use “indirect channels” for “talent poaching, technology theft, and the acquisition of controlled goods” to obtain advanced chipmaking technologies in order to “break through international technological containment.”

“Almost everyone in the industry would know or have heard of people who were approached or worked for Chinese companies,” John Chen, a board director at Taiwan-listed chip design company MicroIP, told Rest of World . “Salary offers often involve five times that in Taiwan. … I have heard it later even went up to 10 times. There are a few friends I know who went to China to work because of that,” said Chen, who has spent nearly four decades in the semiconductor industry. Rest of World ’s review of court filings, combined with interviews with Taiwanese semiconductor engineers, lawyers, and industry insiders, illustrate the efforts Chinese companies have taken to tap Taiwan’s chip sector — and the work that the Taiwanese government has done to fight them off. The Tai Yuen Hi-Tech Industrial Park is made up of 21 office buildings arranged along wide streets on the outskirts of Taiwan’s semiconductor capital Hsinchu. On a weekday afternoon this spring, the sprawling complex, which houses 300 different tech companies, felt quiet and industrious, with only a handful of employees lingering outside a nearby 7-Eleven. The first major raid in the park came in May 2021, less than a year after the MJIB launched the targeted operations. The investigation targeted a Taiwan-registered company tied to the Chinese networking equipment maker Gongjin Electronics. Gongjin initially attempted to register officially with the Taiwanese government, but the registration was rejected by authorities, who alleged that the company had ties to the Chinese military. Subsequently, prosecutors said, Gongjin set up a Taiwan-registered company using a foreign investment structure, listing a Japanese national as its registered representative — although the operational funds still came from China. Registering as a non-Chinese foreign entity or as a foreign person to disguise Chinese affiliations is one of the most common tactics used by Chinese tech companies to hire Taiwanese engineers, Cheng Lun Huang, a senior supervising prosecutor and spokesperson for the Hsinchu District Prosecutors Office, told Rest of World . Cheng Lun Huang, a senior supervising prosecutor for the Hsinchu district, said cases involving Chinese investment in the tech industry are given extra attention. Lam Yik Fei for Rest of World Taiwan has strengthened protection of its semiconductor industry in recent years. In 2022, it tightened the Cross-Strait Act and National Security Act with harsher recommended punishments for offenses. The tougher laws were introduced to protect “critical technologies” and Taiwan’s economic competitiveness, amid a growing number of cases involving Chinese companies’ illegal activities on the island, according to an evaluation report for a legislative proposal passed into law in May that year. The legislative changes came as Beijing accelerated its drive for semiconductor self-reliance. Since unveiling its “ Made in China 2025 ” strategy in 2015, Beijing has poured billions of dollars into building a domestic chip industry through state funding and industrial policies to hit its goal of producing 70% of its chip usage domestically. China’s efforts ramped up even further after Washington restricted Huawei’s access to advanced chips in 2019, followed by sweeping export controls in the years that followed. According to an affiliate of the China Semiconductor Industry Association, the number of Chinese chip design companies grew from 736 in 2015 to 3,901 by 2025. 166 Technology cases investigated by Taiwanese authorities over the past six years for allegedly concealing ties to China. For Taiwan, protecting its semiconductor expertise specifically from Chinese companies has become central to its broader national security strategy as Beijing has intensified military and political pressure and reiterated its goal of “reunification.” This strategy, often referred to as the “silicon shield,” posits that as long as Taiwan remains a critical node for high-end chip manufacturing, the U.S. and its allies would assist in its defense in case of a Chinese attack. Over the past six years, the Hsinchu District Prosecutors Office has been on the frontline of this strategy. The office charged around 60 cases involving nearly 190 individuals claiming illegal business operations, more than any other prosecutor’s office in Taiwan. The industries under review ranged from chip design and semiconductor equipment to AI servers and advanced computing. Huang said cases involving Chinese investment in the tech industry are given extra attention. “We believe foreign investors are watching closely on how well we can protect our intellectual property,” Huang said. MJIB told Rest of World a total of 166 cases alleging illegal Chinese operations and talent poaching have been completed, and that more investigations are ongoing. MJIB declined to provide further details about its operations. However, Rest of World reviewed public court records for 36 of those investigations through Taiwan’s judicial database. All 36 led to convictions for breaching the Cross-Strait Act by operating tech businesses without approval. Thirty-three of these cases focused on companies doing R&D or chip design. The number does not represent all cases that were prosecuted, since there is no public record of cases until judgments are handed down. MJIB told Rest of World it also investigated 67 China-related trade-secret cases in the technology sector over the past six years. When investigations involve allegations more serious than unauthorized business operations, prosecutors may pursue charges under Taiwan’s National Security Act, which criminalizes the theft or unauthorized transfer of “critical technologies,” and carries penalties of up to 12 years in prison and fines of up to 100 million New Taiwan dollars (about $3.1 million). Over the past five years, the Hsinchu District Prosecutors Office has charged around 60 cases involving nearly 190 individuals claiming illegal business operations, more than any other prosecutor’s office in Taiwan. Lam Yik Fei for Rest of World “Whether a company has obtained the required approvals is usually pretty clear,” Hsinchu’s prosecutor Huang told Rest of World . “The threshold for proving a trade secrets violation is much higher,” he said. About 70% of cases involving illegal Chinese operations result in prosecution by his office, Huang said, compared with roughly 20% of trade-secret theft cases. One of the highest-profile cases involved Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , which Taiwanese authorities alleged was behind an unauthorized smartphone chip R&D operation on the island. While the Chinese consumer electronics giant was legally authorized to sell its products in Taiwan, prosecutors said a Xiaomi co-founder directed two former Xiaomi executives to establish a separate chip development business on the island in 2019. They recruited more than two dozen local engineers. According to court documents, Xiaomi’s Beijing subsidiary paid for the research and compensation costs at the Taiwanese operation. In 2024, the two executives — including a former chief financial officer of Beijing-based Xiaomi — were convicted of illegal business operations under the Cross-Strait Act. Xiaomi has not publicly responded to the allegations. A more recent case involved Chinese smartphone brand OnePlus. A court document last November revealed that Taiwanese authorities had issued an arrest warrant for founder Pete Lau, alleging he was involved in operating an unauthorized software R&D outfit on the island that recruited more than 70 engineers in Taiwan. Prosecutors also charged two Taiwanese citizens with allegedly running the operation on Lau’s behalf since 2014. Lau, who is also the senior vice president and chief product officer at OnePlus’ mother company Oppo, did not respond to Rest of World ’s requests for comment. Neither company responded to requests for comment. It has been very challenging for some of my clients to prove they had no awareness, or had no way to verify, whether their investors’ roots were Chinese.” Vincent Huang, an attorney at the Taipei-based WHP law firm MJIB claims that even major Chinese semiconductor firms such as the Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation, or SMIC, China’s most advanced chip foundry, have used a foreign entity to set up a company in Taiwan to poach tech talent. MJIB’s official press release said that SMIC registered as a Samoan company to operate within Taiwan. Few of the Chinese companies linked to these investigations have publicly responded to the allegations. Gongjin Electronics, Xiaomi, and SMIC did not respond to Rest of World ’s requests for comment. Shanghai-listed chip design company VeriSilicon is one of the few Chinese companies to have publicly commented on legal proceedings against it in Taiwan. After Taiwanese authorities raided the company’s Taiwan subsidiary in 2022 over allegations that it had conducted business activities on the island without the required approval, founder and CEO Wayne Dai, in an interview with Chinese media, said the office was merely for sales activities and had never employed engineers or operated chip-testing equipment. VeriSilicon also did not respond to Rest of World ’s questions. As early as 2014, China had a strong incentive to seek overseas technology and talent as its semiconductor industry tried to play “catch up” with global competitors, Hui He, who heads global tech advisory firm Omdia’s semiconductor research in China, told Rest of World . She said many Chinese companies established operations and hired local talent in places such as Taiwan, South Korea, and the U.S. to advance their products while supporting overseas markets. “These moves were largely driven by business needs,” said He. “They were all abiding by market principles. I don’t think they were driven by geopolitical considerations — it is just how the designated location’s legal system interprets these activities,” she said. “Many Western and Taiwanese semiconductor companies are also still operating in China and hiring locals, isn’t it?” Since MJIB started its investigation six years ago, China has made meaningful progress in certain areas of chip design. But in the most cutting-edge chip technology, experts estimate China still lags behind TSMC by anywhere from three to 10 years . Taiwan produces over 60% of the world’s semiconductors. TSMC While Chinese companies still seek expertise to build advanced technology, He said their reliance on poaching foreign talent has diminished in the last three to five years. “There have been more legal restrictions from places like the U.S. and Taiwan,” she said. “China’s semiconductor industry started to have its own talent pool in the last two years, too.” According to available data , it appears that MJIB’s efforts peaked in 2021, the first full year of its campaign, when it raided 100 companies. But authorities have not released sufficient data to determine whether the decline reflects fewer violations or less investigative activity. Taiwan’s industry insiders and legal experts say there is greater general scrutiny and awareness now of China’s involvement in Taiwan’s tech scene than when the MJIB started its targeted crackdown. Vincent Huang, an attorney at the Taipei-based WHP law firm, told Rest of World he has represented more than a dozen clients summoned for questioning by the MJIB in its investigations into illegal Chinese investment. “It has been very challenging for some of my clients to prove they had no awareness, or had no way to verify, whether their investors’ roots were Chinese,” the attorney told Rest of World. “But now, the Taiwanese public is more aware that working for a company backed by Chinese investments could be illegal,” he said . Beyond Taiwan, countries in other regions have also become increasingly alert to Chinese firms’ efforts to acquire critical technologies. The Netherlands, for example, is investigating the national-security implications of the Chinese ownership of Nexperia , a Dutch semiconductor manufacturer which became controlled by Chinese investors through acquisitions. The Dutch and the Chinese governments have been dealing with this issue through diplomatic channels. In the U.S., authorities have prosecuted cases involving Chinese efforts to obtain critical technology, including trade-secret theft by employees at U.S. aerospace technology companies. In January, a former Google engineer was found guilty in a California court for stealing AI trade secrets for a company he founded in China. Nicholas Eftimiades, a former U.S. defense department official whose work included tracking China’s economic espionage, told Rest of World that Chinese companies tailor their approaches to local conditions. In South Korea, for example, Chinese company recruiters would stand outside tech offices to approach exiting workers, he recounted. Eftimiades, who is now a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank, said he believes that the Chinese companies’ methods targeted by the Taiwanese authorities have largely gone unnoticed by the global community. “The technique appears to be … more specific to Taiwan, at least as far as semiconductors go,” he said. “I think the U.S. has got its hands full trying to wrestle with the theft that happens within its own borders.” However, Eftimiades said the U.S. should not take Chinese activities inside Taiwan lightly, even if most of the allegations are not classified under trade-espionage laws. “It has consequences,” he said. “The problem is we lose trillions of dollars in wealth.” MJIB has investigated 166 companies allegedly involved in illegal Chinese business operations in Taiwan since 2020. MJIB “Is it espionage if I sit there poaching talents? Well, in some places it is. We are dealing with different definitions depending on the country, and it’s a problem,” he said, adding that the U.S. should have a coordinated policy with allies like Taiwan. “If the one thing China has proven, it is flexible and resilient. The minute you step on it one way, they turn around and do another,” he said. For some Taiwanese engineers, the fight against talent poaching by Chinese tech companies has become personal. The Hsinchu-based chip designer, who found himself unwittingly working for a Chinese company, said that after leaving Blue Ocean Smart System, he was approached about joining another small chip-design company. He couldn’t find much information about the company and suspected it was another front for a Chinese operation. He didn’t pursue the position. “I made up my mind to not join startups or companies that risk falling into a gray area involving Chinese investments,” he said. Eventually, he got an offer from an American chip design company. This time, he did his due diligence before taking the job. stories.body:
Wong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China

Joshua Wong , one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.

Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.

The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China.

The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.

Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.

In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.

Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.

Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.

Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.

One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings.

“Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.”

In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.

When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.

In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.

Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.

“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.

Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.

“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.

“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.

On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”

Watch: 'I firmly believe I have broken no rules,' Farage tells BBC

Published 2 September 2026, 13:10 BST

Nigel Farage has said the UK is a "complainants' society", as he faces ongoing questions about both his and his party's finances.

Speaking to the BBC ahead of the party's annual conference this week, the Reform UK leader said a "whole ecosystem" didn't want "new kids on the block succeeding".

It comes after a summer dominated by headlines about the party's finances and £5m he received from a party supporter before the last election.

Farage acknowledged his party's poll ratings had taken a hit compared to last year, but said it would rebound and still had "every chance" of winning the next general election.

Reform's annual conference begins in Birmingham on Thursday, with both Farage and the party facing renewed questions over money.

A parliamentary investigation into £5m he received from major Reform donor Christopher Harborne was relaunched following Farage's re-election in Clacton, after a by-election he called in the Essex seat.

The Metropolitan Police is also investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.

The police probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell.

It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received £1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.

'Existential threat'

Asked if he knew whether or not money donated by Fiona Cottrell had come from her son George, Farage said he was not "involved in the transactions".

However, he added that he "had been told it's her money". Reform has insisted it has always complied with donations rules.

He added: "The point is, we live in a complainants' society. If you complain about me, automatically that triggers an investigation."

He said that political parties were "constantly writing to all the authorities", meaning Reform was "under investigation every day for virtually everything we do".

"There's a big picture here. The old two-party system that has dominated since the end of the First World War feels for the first time it faces an existential threat.

"There is a whole ecosystem with a century of development around this. And we come along from virtually nowhere and threaten the whole thing.

"So I think what you're seeing is the establishment, in a very co-ordinated way, fighting back."

Pressed on what he meant, he added: "I'm talking about normal human behaviour.

"People who hold positions of power, influence and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding. It's the whole ecosystem, it's everything."

Farage said he expected it "won't be too long" before he is interviewed by Parliament's standards commissioner Daniel Greenberg as part of his probe into whether he should have publicly declared the £5m he received from Harborne.

He continued to insist the sum, which he says was a personal gift, did not require registration under Commons rules.

He added he had "no questions" about Greenberg's impartiality, but hit out at the "political composition" of the standards committee that will recommend what action should be taken on his findings.

The 14-member panel includes seven MPs from Labour, the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats, but none from Reform UK.

He added: "Have you seen who's on the committee? I think we know the outcome already. I'm not going to say anything more than that."

"To be judged by members of Parliament by other political parties who you're fighting against in by-elections or general elections, I think that raises a question, I really do," he added.

'Fundamental changes'

Elsewhere in his interview, Farage acknowledged that Reform was "down a bit" in its poll ratings compared to 2025, after failing to win in by-elections this year including Gorton and Denton and Makerfield, which saw Andy Burnham's re-election as an MP ahead of becoming Labour leader.

But he added that "markets don't move in straight lines", adding that the party still had "every chance" of winning the next general election, due by 2029.

He said the party was continuing to look "outside of the political sphere" to fill frontbench positions, following a raft of appointments earlier this year to senior posts within the party.

And he said he continued to hold to his previous prediction there would be an election next spring "forced on the government" by the markets, amid rising costs to public borrowing.

Reform's conference, he said, would be a chance for the party to set out details of the "fundamental changes" it would make within 100 days of winning power.

He added that whilst his and other parties had announced a number of new policies in recent weeks, what most interested voters was who is "actually going to deliver" than the specifics of individual policies.

stories.title: Texas and Florida Step Back from ALPRs
stories.summary: Within the last few days, two important state actions have dealt a big blow to automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks. This is just the latest proof of the growing tide of public opposition to mass surveillance. After years of successful grassroots battles to pull these cameras from local streets, bipartisan momentum is sweeping the country. On August 28, Texas Governor Greg Abbott banned state agencies from spending public funds on Flock cameras . The order dropped just as The Texas Tribune prepared to publish an investigation revealing that a state agency had quietly funneled at least $30 million into building a sprawling surveillance network. Then on August 31, the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) issued a memo , announced by Governor Ron DeSantis, ordering the removal of all ALPRs from the right-of-way on state highways within 30 days. The order revokes all previously approved permits to install ALPRs, and bars transportation officials from issuing future permits. FDOT officials stated that “the recent exponential increase in deployments along our roadways, coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes merit immediate action to preserve Floridians’ sovereignty and quality of life.” FDOT’s action has been followed by a surge of local governments in Florida canceling or pausing their vendor contracts . Much more work remains. Many ALPRs in Florida are not on state highways, but sit on city streets, county roads, residential driveways, and shopping center parking lots—and FDOT's order doesn't touch any of them. Likewise, the Texas directive leaves local agencies free to use city, county, federal, and private funds to install cameras. This week’s good news follows years of pushback from local advocates that has seen dozens of cities sever ties with surveillance companies. According to some metrics , during the last 30 days, an average of three localities per day has halted contracts with Flock. Other advocates have been resisting ALPRs in statehouses and court houses , and by blowing the whistle with investigative activism. The moves in Florida and Texas also illustrate the power that the executive branch can wield to curtail mass surveillance with almost immediate results. stories.title: Judge Rules DOD Unlawfully Retaliated Against Anthropic
stories.summary: A federal judge has sided with Anthropic on its claims that the Department of Defense illegally retaliated against Anthropic’s protected speech by labeling the AI company a “supply chain risk.” The judge found that designation, intended to penalize Anthropic for telling the U.S. military it would not allow their technology to be used for mass surveillance of U.S. persons, “constituted unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment.” EFF joined a coalition of organizations in filing multiple amicus briefs ( here , here ) arguing that the Pentagon had trampled on Anthropics First Amendment rights. We agree with the court’s decision and applaud the judge for slapping down such an obvious act of illegal and unconstitutional retribution by the Pentagon—even as the court left open the broader question of whether a company’s choices about how its technology may be used are protected speech in their own right. From the start of this conflict, EFF argued that companies should not be penalized for not wanting to conduct mass surveillance of US persons. Nor do we want to live in a legal system where our susceptibility to surveillance is hashed out and decided in closed-door contract negotiations between a few powerful people at the military and an AI company. Unfortunately, this ruling does little to address the bigger problem: that Congress has abdicated its responsibility to adopt statutory safeguards to protect our privacy, and instead left us reliant on the whims of private companies to decide when they are and are not willing to help the government conduct mass surveillance. In February 2026, the government began threatening to penalize Anthropic unless it backed off its position that it did not want the U.S. military using its AI product Claude for mass surveillance of Americans or to power autonomous weapons systems. Ultimately, the Department of Defense, deciding that it did not want military contractors dictating what its products could or could not be used for, declared the company a “supply chain risk.” This national security designation means the government and companies that do business with it cannot use the company’s products for government projects. stories.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a phenomenon – but there is much more to the gaming world
stories.summary: As Rockstar’s blockbuster prepares to dominate the headlines, it’s time for the mainstream media to stop treating video games as a novelty that needs explaining Predictably, the Grand Theft Auto VI “extended look” which premiered on Netflix last week was a success for all involved. The 30-minute preview scorched to No 1 on the viewing chart and even brought the site down for a few minutes as millions of gamers tried to watch what was, effectively, a very long teaser trailer. According to data collated by Eurogamer , more than 9,000 Twitch streamers covered the show leading to 5,227,798 hours of viewing there alone. And this was just the beginning of what will surely be two months of escalating hype – and unprecedented media attention. Call me cynical, but I suspect the coverage of GTA VI in the media over the next few weeks will follow a familiar pattern. Mostly, it will be five-minute slots wedged in near the end of news bulletins in which games journalists, industry analysts and other pundits will be asked why the game is such a big deal, how much it cost to make and how much revenue it will generate. Perhaps a few will try to reignite the hoary old “violence in video games” debate, there will be presenters laughingly admitting they’ve not touched a game since Pac-Man, rolling their eyes and wallowing in their ignorance, in a way they never would while discussing any other art form. Somebody will venture the subversive view that “games are no longer just for kids”; somebody else will say “games make more money than films and music put together”. And that will be that, job done for another decade … or until there’s a funny story about Pokémon. Continue reading...

stories.title: The Guardian view on the global bond shock: Andy Burnham should take note | Editorial
stories.summary: Japan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieve “In the midst of every crisis lies great opportunity” is an aphorism attributed to Albert Einstein . It seems to be taken to heart by this White House. A global bond sell-off sparked by an inflationary shock emanating from the Gulf sees Donald Trump seeking to restrict plans by Japan – a longtime ally – to reduce dependence on an international system America dominates. Japan, a successful exporter, has long done things its own way. For years Tokyo saw off the bond vigilantes despite running enormous deficits and a huge national debt. Japan’s collision with Donald Trump reveals the dilemma facing Britain: economic independence is becoming more necessary – and more tricky to achieve

“I n the midst of every crisis lies great opportunity” is an aphorism attributed to Albert Einstein . It seems to be taken to heart by this White House. A global bond sell-off sparked by an inflationary shock emanating from the Gulf sees Donald Trump seeking to restrict plans by Japan – a longtime ally – to reduce dependence on an international system America dominates.

Japan, a successful exporter, has long done things its own way. For years Tokyo saw off the bond vigilantes despite running enormous deficits and a huge national debt. It demonstrated how a central bank could fund public spending and keep interest rates low if it wanted to. This economic model was refined by Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister. However, this week the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent , called time on Abenomics as his price for US help in stabilising Japan’s currency. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, he indicated, should shrink her $2tn spending plans and raise rates. Abenomics did not suddenly become financially impossible. It became inconvenient to the issuer of the world’s reserve currency.

Kevin Warsh, Mr Trump’s handpicked chair of the US Federal Reserve, has made it clear that he will raise interest rates in response to inflationary pressures. Others will be expected to follow. In Japan’s case, Washington fears that a yen crisis could become a bond crisis. A disorderly rout could force Japan into ever larger currency interventions – and repeated appeals to Washington to help defend the yen. If such aid proved inadequate, Tokyo could end up defending its currency by dumping US treasury bonds – of which it has more than a trillion dollars worth – and put upward pressure on the very yields Mr Bessent is trying to contain. His demand that Tokyo raise rates and cut spending is not just about Japanese inflation. It is about trying to prevent Tokyo’s adjustment to the Iran shock being exported on to America’s balance sheet.

Mr Burnham’s first Commons speech as prime minister suggests an expansive programme to raise living standards and get growth through regional reindustrialisation. This, he says, rests on the “bedrock” of fiscal responsibility. Mr Burnham promises an activist state to deal with four decades of underinvestment and privatisation. But retaining Rachel Reeves’s fiscal framework leaves his investment plans hostage to interest rates, debt costs and feverish “ headroom ” speculation. Turmoil in global bond markets could derail his industrial strategy before it gets going.

Japan’s big bazooka spending programme was meant to do what Mr Burnham now says Britain must do on a smaller scale: use the state to rebuild productive capacity , reduce strategic dependence and build its export competitiveness. Tokyo has the fiscal firepower, a central bank able to dominate the sovereign bond market and trillions invested overseas. The UK government could mimic that and change its fiscal rules, its relationship to the Bank of England and the way investment is accounted for.

But Japan is Mr Burnham’s problem writ large. The war in Iran made it urgent to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. But the conflict’s inflationary shock makes that objective harder – though not impossible – to pursue. Mr Trump’s team is using its leverage over the yen to restrain Tokyo’s plan to make Japan resilient to external price spikes. Mr Burnham has been forewarned: the Gulf inflation shock wave bolsters the argument for economic independence while making the means of achieving it more difficult.

stories.body:
For Andy Burnham, walking into the bear pit that is Prime Minister’s Questions, it must have been hard to stay calm. His audience was a room of closely packed MPs, some hostile, some friendly – all very loud – many wanting to make a mark.

And the full audience for PMQs extends far beyond the MPs in the chamber. Prime ministers are thinking about the media, external groups, foreign governments, voters and financial markets. The reactions of any of these matter. The PM has the dual worry of dealing with opposition questions while also demonstrating his or her worth to the party members sitting behind them. Backbenchers can signal a lack of confidence through quietness or just not turning up.

It is no wonder that preparing for PMQs is, in itself, demanding. Alastair Campbell, who advised Tony Blair when he was opposition leader and in the early days of the New Labour government, is clear about just what it took . Preparation can take hours. Nerves don’t disappear. And it doesn’t appear to have got any easier in recent years.

Burnham is, of course, new to this. And unlike many in his position, he hasn’t had a chance to rehearse as opposition leader. He was wise to spend part of Tuesday’s return to parliament on a statement and a lengthy question-and-answer session . It gave him a warm-up for the main event.

After Keir Starmer was ousted as prime minister, Labour MPs will be willing Burnham to show that he can succeed. So how did he do in his first PMQs, and what can we glean from it?

Restraint?

This was not a “full-blooded” PMQs. Burham chose not to mount attacks where others might have. A question from Reform UK’s Danny Kruger, for example, could have led to a reply focusing on the party’s reported problems . That it did not, may mean Burnham wants to move away from such attacks – or that he considers Reform less significant than it has been in recent years.

Burnham’s jibes at the Conservatives were not fierce either. He merely criticised past statements made by Tory leader Kemi Badenoch and her shadow cabinet and sought to associate them with the economic failings of past governments. Prime Minister’s Questions is an adversarial event and it will be worth watching whether more obvious hostilities develop in future.

Sharper exchanges in turn end up generating sharper questions, so PMQs could move from point-scoring debate to abusive exchange. But Burnham may have some way to go to match David Cameron, who was identified by researchers as the rudest prime minister at PMQs.

At length

Speaker Lindsay Hoyle warned that Burnham’s long answers may cause the session to overrun. Burnham clearly wanted to spend time on each answer, but this can be a blessing and a curse for a PM. Longer answers mean you can say everything you want. But sometimes the short, sharp reply is most effective at putting your opponent off their stride. The prime minister may have to learn brevity.

Moving on

One of the tricks of dealing with difficult subjects is the “bridge”. That is, taking the topic and linking to something else that you actually do want to talk about. Burnham showed some ability here, linking at one point from a question about public spending to the needs of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets).

His bridge from the Bayeux Tapestry and French president Emmanuel Macron to small boat crossings didn’t work, however. He is clearly a bit rusty in the use of this technique.

Are you listening?

Badenoch was keen to paint the PM as someone who won’t answer questions about spending, and as such as a PM who leans towards more tax and more spend. This may be the beginning of a strategy to frame him as vague and unwilling to commit to specific action in the face of obvious problems. Once an idea like this takes root, it is very hard to shift.

But neither Badenoch nor Burnham has the proper measure of the other yet, and it will take a few more outings before there is a sense of how successful this strategy may prove.

The right man for the job?

As Burnham did not ascend to Downing Street immediately after a run of other roles in parliament, or after a general election, he needed to make his experience clear. He name-checked things he had achieved or initiated, specifically in Greater Manchester, as a way of underlining his credentials.

These references, plus the use of “I”, were designed to demonstrate his ability to get things done, rather like the way it is used in job interviews. Using “I” instead of “my government” or “we” also demonstrates engagement with the topic .

Play nicely

During some replies, Burnham touched on cross-party working, and made an on-the-spot pledge to meet Cornish MPs (not all of whom are Labour) for talks. Offering cross-party working can remove the sting from an attack and make the prime minister seem reasonable. This appears to be a feature of Burnham’s approach and it will be interesting to see if it develops into genuine cooperation with at least some other parties.

Prime ministers often say they want to change aspects of PMQs. Burnham himself has indicated that he wants a different, less Punch-and-Judy tone. Back in 1997, Tony Blair made the move from two shorter sessions a week to one longer one . Blair said he wanted a more considered approach, with more questions and more answers. Whether prime ministers get what they want, of course, is not entirely down to them. They may get the last word, but they don’t control the cast.
